reason: The sources provide over 15 verifiable claims about the expansion of space, Lemaitre's role, and modern cosmological density measurements across multiple independent sites.
story: The Big Bang was not a fireball exploding into a dark void. In 1927, Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre realized that space itself was stretching, suggesting the universe grew from a single primeval atom. Most scientists, including Albert Einstein, initially scoffed. However, Edwin Hubble later proved that galaxies are rushing away from us in every direction. We now know that the Big Bang describes the rapid expansion of space everywhere at once, rather than an explosion in a fixed location. Today, evidence shows our universe is 13.8 billion years old and mostly composed of invisible dark energy and dark matter. Normal atoms, like the ones in your body, make up less than five percent of the cosmos. Recent discoveries by the James Webb Space Telescope are already challenging our models, finding bright galaxies that formed much earlier than anyone thought possible. It was not a bang—it was a silent, universal stretch.
angle: The Big Bang was not an explosion bursting into space, but the stretching of space itself everywhere at once.

claims.claim: Georges Lemaitre proposed that the universe was expanding in 1927.
Lemaitre was a Roman Catholic priest as well as a physicist.
The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old.
The Big Bang represents the intrinsic expansion of space rather than an explosion into a void.
Galaxies are moving away from Earth in all directions.
Dark energy makes up approximately 68 percent of the universe.
Normal matter accounts for less than 5 percent of the universe's density.
Dark matter accounts for roughly 27 percent of the universe.
The universe began in an extraordinarily hot and dense state.
The expansion rate of the universe is a value known as the Hubble constant.
The cosmic microwave background is a snapshot of the universe from roughly 370,000 to 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
Lemaitre called the origin point of the universe the primeval atom.
Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation.
The universe is spatially flat to within a margin of 0.4 percent.
Gravity is a consequence of the warping of space-time by mass.
The James Webb Space Telescope found early galaxies that formed sooner than current models predicted.
Matter could only form after the universe expanded and cooled sufficiently.
Einstein's General Relativity predicted gravitational waves which stretch and squeeze space.
Dark matter halos acted as gravitational sinks that helped form the first galaxies.
Redshift measurements show galaxies receding at speeds proportional to their distance.

disputed: The intent behind the term Big Bang is often reported as pejorative but coiner Fred Hoyle denied this intent [S1, S2].
The exact value of the Hubble constant is under tension as different measurement techniques yield conflicting results [S1, S3].
The timing of early galaxy formation is being debated following JWST observations that contradict standard storybook models [S4].
The initial singularity is treated as a mathematical certainty in general relativity but may be absent in quantum gravity theories [S1, S2].
